title: RBAC, OWASP basics and LLM risks
seriesDescription: AuthN and AuthZ, JWT, OAuth, RBAC, OWASP and LLM risks. JEE-Advanced style: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code and multi-correct questions.
description: Access-control models, injection, XSS, CSRF, CORS and password storage, HTTP security headers, secrets handling, and LLM-specific risks: prompt injection and cross-tenant leaks.
source: OWASP Top 10 (2021, 2025), OWASP API Security Top 10, OWASP Password Storage and CSRF cheat sheets, OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025), MDN (CORS, Strict-Transport-Security), PostgreSQL documentation (PREPARE)

questions.prompt: Match each access-control model to its defining idea.

right.text: Permissions are granted to roles, and users hold roles
Decisions evaluate attributes of user, resource and context
Each object carries a list of who may do what
Access follows relationships in a graph, such as owner or member of
Access is granted by network location only

questions.explanation: Real systems combine them: roles for coarse access, attributes or ownership checks for fine access.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Authorisation must be enforced on the server even when the UI hides forbidden buttons.
questions.reason: Broken Access Control is ranked first (A01) in the OWASP Top 10, in both the 2021 and 2025 editions.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Correct: Both are true, but the ranking is evidence of how common the flaw is, not the reason the check must be server-side: clients can be bypassed.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Hiding UI is usability; checking on the server is security. Missing object-level checks (BOLA) lead the OWASP API Security Top 10 too. In the 2025 edition SSRF was folded into A01 rather than kept as its own category.

questions.prompt: `GET /api/orders/123` returns an order belonging to another customer when a logged-in user simply changes the id. What is the right fix?

options.text: Switch the order ids from integers to random UUIDs and change nothing else.
options.why: Unguessable ids help a little but any leaked id still works.

options.text: Check on the server that the caller may read order 123, every time.
options.why: Correct: an object-level authorisation check on each request.

options.text: Move the id from the URL path into the body of a POST request instead.
options.why: Changing where the id travels does not check who may use it.

options.text: Rate limit the endpoint to ten requests per minute for each user.
options.why: Throttling slows enumeration but still lets one request through.

questions.explanation: BOLA (Broken Object Level Authorization) is API1 in the OWASP API Security Top 10. Enforce it in a shared layer, for example query by `(id, owner)` or a policy check, and test it with two accounts.

questions.prompt: Write PostgreSQL statements that `PREPARE` a statement named `find_user` taking one text parameter and selecting from `users` where `email` equals that parameter, then `EXECUTE` it for `'a@example.com'`.

checks.label: prepares find_user with a text parameter

questions.model:
PREPARE find_user (text) AS SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1;
EXECUTE find_user('a@example.com');
questions.explanation: The parameter is sent separately from the statement text, so a value like `x' OR '1'='1` is just a string. Application drivers do the same with placeholders. Table and column names cannot be parameters: allowlist them.

questions.prompt: The `users` table has 7 rows. Code builds `"SELECT * FROM users WHERE name = '" + input + "'"` and the attacker sends the input `x' OR '1'='1`. How many rows come back?
questions.explanation: The query becomes `WHERE name = 'x' OR '1'='1'`, and the OR condition is true for every row, so all 7 return. The same trick with UNION or stacked statements can read other tables.

questions.prompt: bcrypt's cost factor is a work exponent. How many key-expansion rounds does cost factor 12 perform?
questions.explanation: The work is `2^cost`, so `2^12` = 4096. Each +1 doubles the time, which lets you tune hashing speed as hardware improves.

questions.prompt: Which is the best choice for storing user passwords according to the OWASP Password Storage Cheat Sheet?

options.text: SHA-256 of the password concatenated with a random salt value.
options.why: A fast hash lets attackers test billions of guesses per second.

options.text: Argon2id, with a unique salt for every password.
options.why: Correct: a memory-hard password hash with per-password salt.

options.text: MD5 of the password, hex encoded and stored in the user table.
options.why: MD5 is both fast and broken.

options.text: AES-encrypt the password so that support staff can recover it later.
options.why: Reversible storage means one key theft exposes every password.

questions.explanation: Store only the hash (with the algorithm parameters in the encoded string), re-hash on login when the cost parameters are raised, and never log or email passwords.

questions.prompt: An API key was committed to a git repository and pushed. What is the correct first action?

options.text: Revoke and rotate the key immediately, then clean up the history.
options.why: Correct: once pushed, assume the key is compromised.

options.text: Delete the file in a new commit so the key disappears from the project.
options.why: The key stays in the history and in every clone.

options.text: Make the repository private and wait to see whether anyone uses the key.
options.why: Copies and forks may already exist, and waiting gives attackers time.

options.text: Change the variable name in the code so the key is harder to find.
options.why: Renaming a variable hides nothing from a scan of the history.

questions.explanation: Rotating is the only fix that works; rewriting history is hygiene. Add secret scanning in CI and a pre-commit hook, and load secrets from a secret manager or environment.

questions.prompt: Which measures help against CSRF for a cookie-authenticated web app? Select all that apply.

options.text: `SameSite=Lax` or Strict on the session cookie.
options.why: Correct: the browser withholds the cookie on most cross-site requests.

options.text: A synchroniser or double-submit CSRF token on state-changing requests.
options.why: Correct: a forged request cannot know the token.

options.text: Checking Origin or Referer on unsafe methods.
options.why: Correct: cross-origin requests show a foreign origin.

options.text: Escaping HTML on output.
options.why: Output encoding fights XSS, not forged requests.

options.text: Configuring CORS with `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`.
options.why: A wildcard does not stop forged form posts and weakens isolation.

questions.explanation: Frameworks often enable CSRF protection by default for browser flows; stateless bearer-token APIs often disable it deliberately.

questions.prompt: True or false: a stateless API that authenticates only with an `Authorization: Bearer` header (never cookies) is not vulnerable to classic CSRF.

options.text: True
options.why: Correct: browsers do not attach the header automatically to cross-site requests.

options.text: False
options.why: Classic CSRF relies on the browser sending credentials on its own, which a bearer header does not do.

questions.explanation: The caveat: if the token is kept in a cookie, or XSS can read it, other attacks remain.

questions.prompt: True or false: configuring CORS on the server stops other sites and tools such as curl from calling the API.

options.text: True
options.why: CORS is enforced by browsers; tools ignore it.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: CORS only controls which web origins a browser lets read responses.

questions.explanation: Keep authentication and authorisation on the server. Avoid `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *` together with credentials.

questions.prompt: Write the HTTP response header that tells browsers to use HTTPS only for this host and its subdomains for one year (31536000 seconds).
questions.explanation: HSTS is honoured only when delivered over HTTPS. Add preload only after you are sure every subdomain supports HTTPS. `Content-Security-Policy` and `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` are the other headers interviewers expect.

questions.prompt: Match defence to attack by filling the blanks.
questions.text: Stop XSS with output {1} and a Content-Security-Policy, stop SQL injection with {2} queries, and stop CSRF with SameSite cookies and anti-forgery {3}.
questions.explanation: Defences are specific: encoding fits XSS, parameters fit SQLi, tokens fit CSRF.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Context-aware output encoding is the primary defence against reflected cross-site scripting.
questions.reason: Encoding turns characters such as < and & into harmless text, so the browser does not parse user input as markup or script.

whys.a: Correct: Encoding neutralises the characters that would let input become code in the page.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Choose the encoder for the context (HTML body, attribute, JavaScript, URL), and add a `Content-Security-Policy` as a second layer.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: Blocking the phrase `"ignore previous instructions"` fully prevents prompt injection.
questions.reason: Attackers can paraphrase, translate or encode their instructions.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Not this one: A is true while R is false does not describe this pair; check the truth of R again.
whys.d: Correct: A is false: a phrase filter is easy to evade. R is true and is the reason.

questions.explanation: Treat model output and tool arguments as untrusted, limit the tools the agent can reach, and require confirmation for risky actions.

questions.prompt: Read the assertion A and the reason R, then choose the correct relationship between them.
questions.assertion: In a multi-tenant RAG app the tenant filter must be applied inside the vector search query.
questions.reason: If the system prompt says `"only reveal data for tenant A"`, the model will reliably refuse to expose other tenants' documents.

whys.a: Not this one: Both A and R are true and R explains A does not describe this pair; R does not explain A.
whys.b: Not this one: Both are true but R is not the reason A holds does not describe this pair; R is actually the reason or is false.
whys.c: Correct: A is true because documents must never enter the context. R is false: prompts are not an access control.
whys.d: Not this one: A is false while R is true does not describe this pair; check the truth of A again.

questions.explanation: Enforce isolation before text enters the context: tenant id filter or separate namespace per tenant, then check document ACLs.

questions.prompt: Which controls prevent cross-tenant data leaks in an LLM feature? Select all that apply.

options.text: Apply the tenant id as a mandatory filter or namespace in retrieval.
options.why: Correct: other tenants' text never reaches the context.

options.text: Include the tenant id in semantic-cache keys.
options.why: Correct: a cached answer for tenant A must not be served to tenant B.

options.text: Check each retrieved document against the caller's permissions.
options.why: Correct: finer-grained ACLs still apply inside a tenant.

options.text: Tell the model in the prompt not to mention other tenants.
options.why: Prompts are advice, not enforcement.

questions.explanation: Defence in depth: isolate at retrieval, cache and logging layers; never rely on the model to police access.

questions.prompt: Match each OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications (2025) entry with its title.
questions.explanation: Vector and Embedding Weaknesses is new in 2025 and covers RAG pitfalls such as retrieval ignoring per-user access. Unbounded Consumption covers denial-of-wallet and extraction by heavy querying. Insecure Plugin Design was an entry in the 2023 list.
